records.name: Katsina
records.summary:
For a trans traveler Katsina is primarily a statutory-exposure record: it runs a religious criminal code, in operation since 20 June 2001, and the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force; it is one of only two states/provinces whose law carries death as the maximum penalty for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

Practical safety: no court-case study samples this state/province and no religious-police operation is documented for it, so enforcement here is the bloc-wide pattern rather than a locally documented record; no trans-specific incident is on record.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

Ostien's annotated volume lists Katsina's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, coming into operation on 20 June 2001 and gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23, 27 August 2001, and its annotation records Katsina among the three states (with Kaduna and Kebbi) whose sodomy text reads 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while the lesbianism offence is punished by stoning to death - footnote 183 shows only Kano and Katsina reaching that capital maximum, against the harmonised code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months. Independent academic source for this record's claim that Katsina is one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

records.name: Kebbi
records.summary:
For a trans traveler the practical difference in Kebbi is jurisdictional: it runs a parallel religious criminal code - in operation since 1 December 2000 - that applies to Muslims, with death by stoning as the maximum for men's same-sex acts and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to six months for same-sex acts between women; the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Practical safety: for a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, exposure is to a religious court applying a criminal code broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the national statute alone - the code extends criminalisation to acts between women that the national law does not reach; no enforcement record against trans people specific to this state/province exists.

sources.summary: HRW 2004 report, chapter IV 'The extension of Shari'a to criminal law': Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve northern states - Kebbi among them - had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states with such jurisdiction.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3): Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21) (2000) with death by stoning for liwat (sodomy) and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to 6 months for same-sex acts between women - the standard bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano/Katsina capital maximum. Dated government confirmation that Kebbi's Sharia layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, matching this record's claim that the state's code is broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Ostien's annotated volume lists Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed into law and coming into operation on 1 December 2000 (Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000), and its annotations record Kebbi as one of three states (with Kaduna and Katsina) whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while lesbianism follows the harmonised code's 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Enactment-level confirmation that Kebbi adopted its own Sharia penal layer in the 1999-2002 wave with a capital ceiling for men's acts and women's same-sex conduct criminalised, grounding this record's jurisdictional-difference finding in Kebbi's own statute.

records.name: Niger
records.summary:
For a trans traveler Niger State adds a parallel religious criminal track for Muslim defendants: the penal code amendment law of this state/province - in operation since 4 May 2000 - provides that a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the religious evidentiary standard receives the harsher religious-specified punishment, while the ordinary national-code punishment applies otherwise; the June 2025 government note confirms the religious layer remains in force and extends criminalisation to acts between women.

Practical safety: an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under national law alone, under a parallel jurisdiction that states/provinces outside the religious bloc do not have; no enforcement record against trans people specific to this state/province is documented.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

The annotated sourcebook catalogue records Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, HB.4/2000, signed into law on 22 February 2000 and coming into operation on 4 May 2000 (Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8, 9 March 2000). The editor notes it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it merely amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. Confirms the state-specific enactment behind this record's claim that an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

records.name: Imo
records.summary:
In Imo, enforcement under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law is active: in February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the law with its 14-year term, expressly framing the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'. The parallel risk is community violence: in April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them, and a follow-up inquiry records that police took the two men into custody.

For a discovered visitor the risk comes from neighbours and police alike: mob justice drew no recorded accountability in 2018, while named command-level enforcement invoked the criminal law in 2025. No visitor documents or border-screening practice, and no marriage or partner-travel provision, is recorded in the dossier for this state.

sources.summary: 76crimes (26 Apr 2018): two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found the victims were themselves arrested by police and may need legal support. Documents community vigilantism plus police processing of the accused.

Nigerian Newspoint (19 Feb 2025): Imo Police Command foiled a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe (Owerri West), arrested many gay and lesbian suspects, with fleeing attendees on a police search list. Evidence of active 2025 police enforcement against same-sex gatherings in Imo.
